subject: Neurology
vignette: A 62-year-old man is brought by his family for progressive behavioral changes over 18 months. He has become socially disinhibited, overeats to the point of gaining 15 kg, and shows no concern when his wife becomes tearful. He cannot plan his finances or sequence his morning routine. MRI shows marked atrophy of the frontal and temporal poles.
question: Which of the following best describes the most likely lesion and associated syndrome?

options.text: Bilateral amygdala lesions causing Klüver-Bucy syndrome
Prefrontal cortex degeneration causing frontal lobe syndrome (frontotemporal dementia)
Mammillary body damage causing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Hippocampal atrophy causing anterograde amnesia (Alzheimer disease)
Dorsal midbrain compression causing Parinaud syndrome

explanation_correct: The prefrontal cortex mediates executive function, impulse control, empathy, and feeding behavior. Bilateral prefrontal degeneration produces frontal lobe syndrome —disinhibition, hyperphagia, impulsivity, loss of empathy, impaired executive function, and in severe cases akinetic mutism—and is the characteristic presentation of frontotemporal dementia. The MRI showing frontal and temporal pole atrophy supports this localization.

explanation_incorrect.A: Klüver-Bucy syndrome from bilateral amygdala lesions also features hyperphagia and disinhibition, but it is distinguished by hypersexuality and hyperorality and is classically due to HSV-1 encephalitis rather than slowly progressive frontotemporal atrophy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mammillary body lesions cause Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency, with anterograde amnesia, confabulation, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, not the isolated behavioral disinhibition described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bilateral hippocampal damage causes an inability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia), as in Alzheimer disease; executive function and empathy are relatively preserved early in that condition.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) lesions from pineal mass effect cause vertical gaze palsy and pupillary light-near dissociation, not a progressive personality and behavior change.

educationalObjective: Prefrontal cortex degeneration produces frontal lobe syndrome with disinhibition, hyperphagia, impulsivity, and loss of empathy—the hallmark of frontotemporal dementia.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 68-year-old man develops sudden right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. On examination he has right hemiplegia and does not turn his eyes toward the examiner when called from the right; his eyes are deviated to the left. CT shows a left middle cerebral artery territory infarct.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's gaze deviation?

options.text: A left paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) lesion, because the eyes look away from a brainstem lesion
A right frontal eye field lesion, because the eyes look toward the contralateral hemisphere
A left frontal eye field lesion, because the eyes look toward the side of the lesion and away from the hemiplegia
A right frontal eye field lesion, because the eyes look away from the side of the lesion
A left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia

explanation_correct: The frontal eye fields initiate voluntary contralateral gaze. A destructive left frontal eye field lesion removes the drive to look right, leaving the intact right frontal eye field to deviate the eyes to the left—toward the lesion and away from the hemiplegia. This conjugate gaze preference is typical of MCA territory strokes involving the frontal eye fields.

explanation_incorrect.A: A PPRF lesion makes the eyes look away from the brainstem lesion, ie, toward the hemiplegia, the opposite of this patient's leftward gaze with right hemiplegia; the lesion here is supratentorial.
explanation_incorrect.B: A right frontal eye field lesion would deviate the eyes to the right (toward that lesion), not to the left as seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: A right frontal eye field lesion would produce rightward gaze deviation with left hemiplegia, the reverse of these findings.
explanation_incorrect.E: A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia—impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye—not a conjugate gaze preference.

educationalObjective: A frontal eye field lesion deviates the eyes toward the side of the lesion and away from the side of the hemiplegia (classically with MCA stroke).

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman develops an acute brainstem stroke. Examination shows a conjugate gaze palsy: her eyes rest deviated to the right and she cannot voluntarily look to the left. She also has left-sided weakness. MRI shows an acute infarct in the left pontine tegmentum involving the paramedian pontine reticular formation.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected direction of gaze deviation with a destructive lesion at this site?

options.text: Eyes look away from the lesion, toward the side of the hemiplegia
Eyes look toward the lesion, away from the side of the hemiplegia
Eyes deviate downward with loss of vertical gaze only
The ipsilateral eye fails to adduct while the contralateral eye abducts with nystagmus
Eyes deviate toward the lesion with preserved voluntary vertical gaze

explanation_correct: The PPRF is the horizontal gaze center of the pontine tegmentum; it drives ipsilateral gaze by exciting the adjacent abducens nucleus. A destructive PPRF lesion therefore makes the eyes deviate away from the brainstem lesion—which, when the corticospinal tract is also involved, is toward the side of the hemiplegia. This is the opposite of a frontal eye field lesion.

explanation_incorrect.B: Eyes looking toward the lesion and away from the hemiplegia is the pattern of a frontal eye field (cortical) lesion, not a PPRF lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Isolated loss of vertical gaze with downward deviation suggests dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome from pineal compression, not a pontine PPRF lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failure of ipsilateral adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus is internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gaze toward the lesion is characteristic of a frontal eye field lesion; a destructive PPRF lesion directs gaze away from the lesion.

educationalObjective: A PPRF lesion causes the eyes to look away from the brainstem lesion and toward the side of the hemiplegia—the reverse of frontal eye field lesions.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 67-year-old right-handed man is evaluated for difficulty writing and calculating. He can see and speak normally but cannot write simple sentences, cannot perform mental arithmetic, cannot identify his own fingers when touched, and confuses left and right. MRI shows a lesion in the dominant parietal lobule.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hemispatial neglect syndrome
Klüver-Bucy syndrome
Wernicke aphasia
Gerstmann syndrome
Ideomotor apraxia

explanation_correct: Gerstmann syndrome results from a lesion of the dominant (usually left) parietal cortex, particularly the angular gyrus, and consists of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation. The patient's four deficits map exactly onto this tetrad, and the dominant parietal location on MRI confirms it.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hemispatial neglect follows nondominant (right) parietal lesions and produces agnosia of the contralateral side of the world, not an agraphia/acalculia/finger agnosia tetrad.
explanation_incorrect.B: Klüver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral amygdala lesions and produces hyperorality, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia, not these parietal signs.
explanation_incorrect.C: Wernicke aphasia is a fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension from a dominant superior temporal lesion; finger agnosia and left-right disorientation are not its defining features.
explanation_incorrect.E: Apraxia refers to impaired execution of learned motor acts despite intact strength and sensation and does not account for the full tetrad including acalculia and finger agnosia.

educationalObjective: Dominant parietal lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome—agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 70-year-old right-handed woman has a right hemisphere stroke. She has left-sided weakness but, more strikingly, she ignores the left half of her world: she eats only food on the right side of her plate, does not dress her left arm, and denies that her left hand belongs to her.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: A lesion of the dominant (left) parietal cortex causing Gerstmann syndrome
A lesion of the nondominant (right) parietal cortex causing hemispatial neglect syndrome
A lesion of the left frontal eye field causing gaze deviation
Bilateral hippocampal lesions causing anterograde amnesia
A lesion of the cerebellar vermis causing truncal ataxia

explanation_correct: The nondominant (usually right) parietal cortex attends to both sides of space; when it is damaged, the contralateral (left) side of the world is ignored, producing hemispatial neglect. Patients may fail to eat, dress, or acknowledge stimuli on the neglected side, as in this vignette. Gerstmann syndrome is the contrasting dominant parietal syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dominant parietal lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation), not neglect of the contralateral world.
explanation_incorrect.C: A left frontal eye field lesion causes conjugate gaze deviation toward the lesion, not multimodal inattention to left-sided stimuli.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bilateral hippocampal lesions impair formation of new memories without causing spatial neglect or unilateral inattention.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cerebellar vermis lesions cause truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait, not neglect.

educationalObjective: Nondominant parietal lesions cause hemispatial neglect—agnosia of the contralateral side of the world—whereas dominant parietal lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 34-year-old woman develops a severe encephalitic illness with fever and headache. After recovery she is markedly changed: she is docile, has an insatiable appetite, repeatedly puts objects in her mouth, and displays inappropriate sexual behavior. MRI shows destructive lesions of the bilateral temporal lobes including the amygdalae.
question: Which of the following best accounts for this behavioral syndrome?

options.text: Bilateral mammillary body damage from thiamine deficiency
Bilateral subthalamic nucleus damage from a vascular lesion
Bilateral hippocampal damage from chronic hypoxia
Dorsal midbrain compression from a pineal gland tumor
Bilateral amygdala destruction, classically due to HSV-1 encephalitis

explanation_correct: Bilateral amygdala lesions produce Klüver-Bucy syndrome—docility, disinhibition, hyperphagia, hypersexuality, hyperorality, and visual agnosia. HSV-1 encephalitis has a tropism for the medial temporal lobes, orbitofrontal cortex, and amygdala, making it the classic infectious cause. This patient's hyperorality, hypersexuality, and hyperphagia fit the syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Mammillary body lesions cause Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency, characterized by anterograde amnesia, confabulation, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, not Klüver-Bucy behaviors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Subthalamic nucleus lesions cause contralateral hemiballismus with violent proximal limb movements, not a behavioral disinhibition syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) without hyperorality or hypersexuality.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dorsal midbrain compression by a pineal tumor causes Parinaud syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, not the behavioral changes of Klüver-Bucy syndrome.

educationalObjective: Bilateral amygdala destruction (classically HSV-1 encephalitis) causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome with hyperphagia, hypersexuality, and hyperorality.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with a wide-based, unsteady gait and a tendency to fall. He has nystagmus and slurred speech, but no limb ataxia or intention tremor when reaching for objects.
question: Which of the following best localizes the lesion responsible for this patient's truncal ataxia?

options.text: The cerebellar hemisphere on the side toward which he falls
The dorsal midbrain near the pineal gland
The cerebellar vermis, which is centrally located and affects the midline trunk
The frontal eye fields of the dominant hemisphere
The subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the affected limbs

explanation_correct: The cerebellar vermis is the midline portion of the cerebellum and controls axial (truncal) stability; its degeneration, classically from chronic alcohol overuse, produces truncal ataxia with a wide-based —drunken sailor— gait, nystagmus, and dysarthria. Because the vermis is centrally located, it affects the central body rather than individual limbs, matching this patient's gait and speech findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: The laterally located cerebellar hemispheres affect the ipsilateral limbs, producing intention tremor, limb ataxia, and falling toward the side of the lesion—findings absent here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dorsal midbrain lesions cause Parinaud syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, not truncal ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Frontal eye field lesions cause conjugate gaze deviation, not gait ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Subthalamic nucleus lesions cause contralateral hemiballismus, not a wide-based gait.

educationalObjective: Vermis lesions cause truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait (chronic alcohol use), whereas cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor.
